name: AddressSanitizer (LLVM compiler-rt)
workload: Memory-error detection (heap/stack/global buffer overflow, use-after-free) on SPEC CPU2006 C/C++ programs.
claimed_speedup: About 2x slowdown for AddressSanitizer versus about 20x for Valgrind/Memcheck and about 10x for Dr. Memory (comparison table); own SPEC CPU2006 run: average slowdown 1.93, median 1.86, range 1.12x (462.libquantum) to 3.79x (400.perlbench).
hardware: Intel Xeon W3690 @ 3.47GHz (own-numbers page only; the comparison table does not state hardware)
stars_or_usage: Shipped in GCC and Clang; google/sanitizers docs repo 12.5k stars (archived, code lives in llvm-project compiler-rt)
tradeoffs: Needs recompilation with the sanitizer (compiler instrumentation, not binary instrumentation); roughly 2x memory use; cannot check uninstrumented libraries; different bug classes than Memcheck (no uninitialized-read detection, that is MemorySanitizer).
caveats: Comparison table slowdowns for Valgrind and Dr. Memory are quoted from a published Dr. Memory paper, not rerun on the same machine; the ASan-only numbers are from 2013 on Clang 3.3 and the Valgrind column has no stated flags or CPU. Peer-reviewed USENIX ATC 2012 paper exists but was not reachable (arXiv/ACM/USENIX not opened), so tier stays C. The canonical code path is compiler-rt inside llvm-project; confirm whether llvm-project is already catalogued.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'sampling-based tool faster than Valgrind' then github.com/google/sanitizers wiki pages

name: Dr. Memory
workload: Memory-error checking (uninitialized reads, heap errors, leaks) of unmodified binaries on SPEC CPU2006, Linux.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Dr. Memory is faster than comparable tools, including Valgrind, as shown in our CGO 2011 paper'; ASan comparison table lists Dr. Memory at about 10x slowdown vs Valgrind/Memcheck about 20x (derived from the quoted paper data).
tradeoffs: Built on DynamoRIO dynamic instrumentation, no recompilation; still roughly 10x slower than native; runs on Windows, Linux, Mac, Android.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (CGO 2011 'Practical Memory Checking with Dr. Memory') but the paper and its chart were not opened; the README only shows a chart and qualitative statement. The 10x vs 20x figures come from the AddressSanitizer comparison wiki, which cites the paper. License string from README/GitHub summary reported as LGPL; exact SPDX variant not verified.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch sampling-based tool faster than Valgrind; HN title 'Dr. Memory: A Memory Checker Faster Than Valgrind'

name: Coz causal profiler
workload: Profiling overhead on Phoenix suite programs and pbzip2 and other benchmarks; causal profiling of native C/C++/Rust code (not a plain speed claim).
claimed_speedup: Search snippet of the SOSP 2015 paper: mean overhead 17% (min 0.1%, max 65%), versus gprof up to 6x overhead (snippet only, not seen on a page I opened).
tradeoffs: Needs progress points in source (or latency points) and debug info; Linux and macOS; Python 3 for the viewer; it answers a different question (what to optimize) than gprof or perf.
caveats: Overhead numbers come only from a WebSearch snippet of the paper (arxiv.org/pdf/1608.03676 blocked by egress); the repo README has no comparative numbers. Overhead comparison is to gprof's instrumentation cost, not a like-for-like profile. Verifier needs paper access.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'Coz causal profiler github plasma-umass coz overhead evaluation'

name: E9Patch
workload: Static x86_64 binary rewriting for instrumentation; basic-block counting overhead on SPEC-style benchmarks and rewrite time on large binaries (Chrome, Firefox).
claimed_speedup: Search snippet of the PLDI 2020 paper: Dyninst about 70% overhead for basic-block counting vs PEBIL 62%, Multiverse 60.48% (E9Patch's own figure not captured); README: rewrites most binaries in a few seconds and -O2 output sometimes 2x faster than earlier versions.
tradeoffs: x86_64 Linux ELF only; GPL-3.0; tool-building framework rather than a ready profiler; binaries grow with trampolines.
caveats: Baseline named in the snippet is Dyninst (not in this category's baseline list); no direct comparison to perf, gprof or Valgrind was seen. Paper PDF (comp.nus.edu.sg) was blocked by egress, numbers are snippet-only and E9Patch's own overhead is not captured. Verifier should read the PLDI paper.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'E9Patch static binary rewriting faster than Valgrind Dyninst overhead'

name: RetroWrite
workload: Binary-only AddressSanitizer for stripped x86_64 binaries and AFL coverage instrumentation, versus Valgrind memcheck and QEMU-mode AFL.
claimed_speedup: Search snippet of the IEEE S&P 2020 paper: binary-only ASan 3x faster than Valgrind memcheck while detecting 80% more bugs; coverage instrumentation identical to compiler-instrumented and 4.5x faster than QEMU (snippet only).
tradeoffs: Works only on position-independent (PIE) x86_64 and aarch64 Linux binaries with symbolization limits; the tool itself is Python but its output is ordinary assembler, so result binaries are usable from C++ workflows.
caveats: Numbers only from a WebSearch snippet; nebelwelt.net and ieeexplore were blocked by egress. The repo README makes only a qualitative 'zero overhead' claim. Verifier should read the S&P 2020 paper evaluation section.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'RetroWrite binary rewriting coverage instrumentation faster than QEMU Valgrind sanitizer'

name: heaptrack
workload: Heap allocation profiling with stack traces on real applications, compared with Valgrind's massif.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only: multi-threaded programs are not serialized, and time and memory overhead are 'significantly lower' than Valgrind; a search snippet of the author's blog says about 10x faster (not on a page I opened).
tradeoffs: LD_PRELOAD interposition on allocator calls (Linux only); records every allocation so trace files can grow large; no CPU profiling.
caveats: No numbers in the repo; license not read directly (repo uses a REUSE LICENSES directory), so SPDX id left null for the verifier. Tier D kept as the single notable no-numbers entry.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'efficient memory profiler lower overhead than Valgrind massif heaptrack'
